t: Check if Point Is Reachable — GCD Invariant
o: From (1,1) we may replace (x,y) by (x, y-x), (x-y, y), (2x, y), or (x, 2y). We must decide whether (targetX, targetY) is reachable. Example 1: gcd(6,9)=3, not a power of two, so unreachable. Example 2: gcd(4,7)=1 = 2^0, reachable. Coordinates go up to 1e9, so any search over states is hopeless — we need a closed-form criterion.
k: The subtraction moves are Euclidean-algorithm steps: they preserve gcd(x, y).
Doubling one coordinate multiplies the gcd by 2, so starting from gcd 1 the gcd can only ever become a power of 2.
Conversely, any pair whose gcd is a power of 2 is reachable: divide out the 2s, then run the Euclidean algorithm backwards to reach (1,1).

a.i: Reachability holds iff gcd(targetX, targetY) is a power of two. Necessity follows from the invariants above; sufficiency follows because halving both coordinates repeatedly reduces to a pair with odd gcd 1, and reversing Euclid's algorithm from any coprime pair reaches (1,1) using only subtractions, while the removed factors of 2 are produced by doubling moves.
s: While g is even, divide g by 2.

a.i: Same criterion derived constructively: strip common factors of 2 by halving, then repeatedly replace the larger number by the difference (Euclid) until both equal 1; every step reverses to a legal forward move, proving reachability without invoking the invariant argument abstractly.
s: While both coordinates are even, halve them.
While (x, y) != (1, 1), replace the larger by |x - y| (this mirrors a reversed subtraction move).
If you end at (1,1) the original was reachable; this happens exactly when the original gcd was a power of two.
a.t: O(log^2(max)) — repeated subtraction Euclid; still instant for 1e9.

w: Lead with the gcd-power-of-two insight; it turns a Hard search problem into a one-liner. Pitfall: trying BFS/DFS on states — the state space is astronomically large. Follow-up: prove sufficiency formally (reverse Euclid + doublings), or ask which points are reachable in exactly k moves.
